messages.content: Explain in exactly three sentences why floating-point addition is not associative.
Explain in exactly three sentences why floating-point addition is not associative.

samples.text: Floating‑point numbers have a finite precision, so each operation rounds the exact real result to the nearest representable value. When you add three numbers, the rounding can occur after the first two operands or after the second two operands, and the two intermediate rounded results can differ. Because those differences affect the final rounding, (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can produce distinct floating‑point values, breaking associativity.

Floating‑point numbers have a finite precision, so each operation rounds the exact real result to the nearest representable value. When you add three numbers, rounding after the first addition can change the magnitude of the intermediate result, causing a different rounding error than if you round after the second addition. Consequently, (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can produce different floating‑point results, breaking associativity.

Floating‑point numbers have a finite precision, so each operation rounds the exact real result to the nearest representable value. When you add three numbers, rounding after the first addition can change the magnitude of the intermediate sum, causing a different rounding error than if you round after the second addition. Consequently, (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can produce different floating‑point results, showing that addition is not associative in floating‑point arithmetic.

Floating‑point numbers have a finite precision, so each operation rounds the exact real result to the nearest representable value. When you add three numbers, rounding after the first addition can discard small bits that would affect the later addition, whereas rounding after a different grouping may retain them. Consequently, (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can produce different rounded results, breaking associativity.

Floating‑point numbers have a finite precision, so each operation rounds the exact real result to the nearest representable value. When you add three numbers, the rounding can occur after the first addition (a + b) and again after the second addition ((a + b) + c), producing a different rounded result than if you first add b + c and then add a. Because the intermediate rounding errors depend on the grouping, the final stored sum can differ, breaking the associativity property.

When you add three numbers, rounding after the first addition can change the magnitude of the intermediate result, causing a different rounding error than if you round after the second addition. Consequently, \((a+b)+c\) and \(a+(b+c)\) can produce different floating‑point results, showing that addition is not associative in floating‑point arithmetic.

Because the intermediate rounding errors depend on the grouping, (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can yield different floating‑point values, breaking associativity.
